| Who may cross it? | `sys_transition_access`, from `rbac` | bypasses it |

So an edge no access rule names is open to any authenticated caller, while an
edge the machine omits is refused to everyone. `GET /api/workflows/transitions`
returns the stored edges (narrowed by `?table=` and `?from=`), so a screen can
offer only the moves that exist. A table with no machine has no rows, and
nothing is enforced for it.

### 5.3 Sagas

A saga is a process that takes several steps, touches more than one entity, and
carries values from one step to the next: escalate a deviation and open a CAPA,
convert a qualified lead, admit a patient.

```yaml
sagas:
  - name: CriticalDeviationEscalation
    entity: DeviationReport
    trigger: rule
    steps:
      - id: B
        type: Formula
        label: Stage base days
        properties: { target: baseDays, operation: set, value: "3" }
      - id: C
        type: Formula
        label: Compute resolution days
        properties: { target: resolutionDays, source: baseDays, operation: multiply, operand: "7" }
      - id: D
        type: CreateEntity
        label: Open a CAPA
        properties:
          entity: Capa
          as: newCapaId
          fields: '{"title":"CAPA for deviation {{id}}","status":"open","deviation_report_id":"{{id}}"}'
      - id: E
        type: UpdateEntity
        label: Escalate the deviation
        properties: { field: status, value: escalated }
      - id: F
        type: UpdateEntity
        label: Carry the window onto the CAPA
        properties: { entity: Capa, targetSource: newCapaId, field: effectiveness_metric, source: resolutionDays }
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **`name`**, `title`, `description` | What the saga is. |
| **`entity`** | The entity whose writes start it. |
| `trigger` | `automatic` (default) or `rule`. |
| `operation` | `CREATE` (default), `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `ALL` — which write starts it, for `trigger: automatic`. |
| **`steps`** | `{ id, type, label?, properties? }`, run in the order listed (`EML430` when empty). `id` is unique in the saga (`EML270`); every property value is a string. |

#### The trigger

| `trigger` | Runs |
|---|---|
| `automatic` | on every write to the entity that matches `operation` |
| `rule` | only when a rule's `trigger-workflow` action names it — the rule's `when` decides |

Choose `rule` whenever the saga should not run on every write: it is what makes
a condition load-bearing. A rule-triggered saga that no action names can never
run (`EML286`).

The generated Loco backend currently starts a saga only through a rule's
`trigger-workflow` action or `POST /api/workflow/{id}/execute`. `trigger:
automatic` is recorded on the definition (`sys_workflow_definitions.trigger_type`)
and not yet acted on by that backend.

#### Passing values between steps

Steps share one context: the triggering record's columns, plus every variable an
earlier step published. `CreateEntity` publishes the new row's id under `as`;
`Formula` under `target`; `Decision` one variable per output column of the row
that matched. A later step reads one by naming it in `source` or `targetSource`,
or as `{{name}}` inside `fields`. A step reading a variable no earlier step
publishes is `EML264`. Without this a saga could insert a row and never reach it
again.

#### Step types

The single source of truth is `workflowConstructs.stepNodes` in the language
definition; the checker, both generators, the modelling tool and the generated
Workflow Designer all read it.

| Type | Requires | Optional | Does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `UpdateEntity` | `field`, and `source` or `value` | `entity`, `targetField`, `targetSource` | writes one column |
| `CreateEntity` | `entity`, `fields` | `as` | inserts a row, publishing its id |
| `DeleteEntity` | — | `entity`, `targetField`, `targetSource`, `hard` | soft-deletes (stamps `deleted_at`); `hard: "true"` removes the row |
| `Decision` | `decisionTable` or `rule` | `publish` | evaluates a decision table and publishes its outputs |
| `Formula` | `target`, `operation` | per operation | publishes a value into the context |
| `REST` | `url` | `method`, `bodyTemplate` | calls an external endpoint; `bodyTemplate` interpolates `{{key}}` |
| `Agent` | `agentId` | — | not shipped: the executor logs and skips it |

An unknown type is `EML261`, a missing property `EML262`, an unknown one
`EML268`, and a step naming an undeclared entity `EML266`.

**`fields`** (`CreateEntity`) is a JSON object of column → context key or
literal, written as a YAML string; a string naming a context key is substituted
(`EML267` when it is not a JSON object).

**`Formula`** operations: `multiply`, `divide`, `add`, `subtract` need `source`
and `operand`, both read as numbers; `set` needs `value`, stored unchanged — the
only way to pass text to a later step; `copy` needs `source`, carried across
unchanged.

**`Decision`** puts a decision table inside the process. `decisionTable` is the
table itself as JSON — `{ hitPolicy, inputs, outputs, rules }` — for logic only
this process needs; `rule` names a rule declared elsewhere in the model
(`EML273` when it is not), when the same table already governs the entity.
`publish` narrows what is published to a comma-separated list. A table that
matches no row publishes nothing — that is how "leave it alone" is said, and the
steps that would have read its variables skip themselves. **Every row must set
every output column**: the engine discards a row that leaves one unset, and one
such row stops the whole table matching (`EML272`; `EML271` for a table that is
not valid JSON).

**Row targeting** (`UpdateEntity`, `DeleteEntity`): with no `entity` the step
acts on the triggering record. To reach another entity, set `entity` and either
`targetSource` (a context key holding the row id) or `targetField` (a foreign key
matched against the triggering row). Targeting another entity with neither is
refused rather than guessed (`EML265`) — updating the wrong row is bad, deleting
it is worse.

#### What a saga generates

One row in `sys_workflow_definitions`, holding BPMN with one `bpmn:serviceTask`
per step in the order listed, and `trigger_type` from `trigger`. Definitions
from the model carry `source: 'model'`: **the model owns them** — regeneration
rewrites them, and the generated Workflow Designer shows them read-only.
Workflows authored in the application carry `source: 'designer'` and are never
touched by regeneration, so the two cannot overwrite each other.

#### Compensation

A saga that needs rollback pairs each forward step with a compensating one — a
`DeleteEntity` undoing a `CreateEntity`, an `UpdateEntity` restoring a prior
value. The executor runs a linear chain, so compensation is written as explicit
steps; automatic compensating-transaction orchestration is not part of the
language.

### 5.4 Automations

An automation is the form a workflow takes when it is built in the automation
builder — in the modelling tool and in a generated application. It is one
sentence:

> When a `DeviationReport` **is created**, only if `severity` **is** `critical`,
> look up the escalation tier, create a CAPA, and write the tier back.

A trigger, a flat list of conditions that must all pass, and an ordered list of
steps. There is deliberately no graph: the executor runs steps in order and stops
at the first failure, so a list is the honest representation. It is a profile of
the saga's step machinery, not a second language.

Each automation is its own YAML document, stored in
`sys_workflow_definitions.definition_yaml` (and, in the modelling tool, in the
project's history under `model/automations/`). The backend refuses a document of
any other shape.

```yaml
automation: "1.0"
name: Escalate critical deviations
kind: automation
trigger:
  entity: DeviationReport
  event: created
conditions:
  - { id: c1, field: severity, operator: eq, value: critical }
loops: []
steps:
  - id: s1
    type: Decision
    resultName: tier
    props: { ruleTable: Escalation tier }
  - id: s2
    type: CreateEntity
    resultName: capaId
    props: { entity: CAPA }
  - id: s3
    type: UpdateEntity
    resultName: ""
    props: { field: status, value: "{{tier}}" }
hooks: []
status: live
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `automation` | The document version, `"1.0"`. |
| `name`, `description` | What it is called. |
| `kind` | `automation`, `hook` (a hook workflow: its rungs are hooks) or `saga`. |
| `trigger` | `{ entity, event }`. |
| `sagaTrigger`, `sagaOperation` | For `kind: saga`: as a saga's `trigger` and `operation`. |
| `conditions` | `{ id, field, operator, value }`, all of which must pass. |
| `loops` | `{ id, condition, maxPasses }`. |
| `steps` | `{ id, type, resultName, props, loopId?, table? }`, in order. |
| `hooks` | For `kind: hook`: `{ id, event, handler, field? }`. |
| `status` | `draft`, `live` or `paused`. |

Keys are written in a fixed order and nothing that belongs to the screen is
stored, so saving an automation twice writes the same bytes. The same reader and
writer (`lib/automation/yaml.ts`) ship in the modelling tool and in every
generated application, byte for byte.

#### Triggers

The events are the lifecycle hooks the generated services already fire, named
the way someone describing their business would name them:

| `event` | Hook | Can still block the write |
|---|---|---|
| `created` | `afterCreate` | no |
| `beforeCreated` | `beforeCreate` | yes |
| `updated` | `afterUpdate` | no |
| `beforeUpdated` | `beforeUpdate` | yes |
| `deleted` | `afterDelete` | no |
| `beforeDeleted` | `beforeDelete` | yes |

#### Conditions

All must pass; there is no OR and no nesting — an author who needs alternatives
writes a second automation, which stays readable where a boolean tree does not.
No conditions means the automation always runs. Operators: `eq`, `neq`, `gt`,
`gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `contains`, `startsWith`, `isEmpty`, `isNotEmpty`,
`changed`; the last three take no value.

#### Steps and references

| Type | Properties | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `Decision` | `ruleTable`, `inputs` | evaluates a rule table and publishes its outputs |
| `CreateEntity` | `entity`, `values` | creates a record on another entity |
| `UpdateEntity` | `entity`, `field`, `value` | writes a field, by default on the triggering record |
| `DeleteEntity` | `entity`, `target` | removes a record |
| `Formula` | `operation`, `left`, `right` | computes a value and publishes it |
| `REST` | `method`, `url`, `body` | calls an external service |

A step reads, in double braces, a field of the triggering record
(`{{deviationreport.severity}}`, the entity name lower-cased) or the published
result of an earlier step (`{{tier}}`, by its `resultName`). Resolution is
positional — a step sees only what precedes it — which is what makes the list
safe to reorder.

A saga-kind automation composes into the model when the project is generated:
its steps become a `sagas` entry, translated at that one edge (`values` →
`fields`, a Formula's `left`/`right` → `source`/`operand`, `{{name}}` → a bare
`source`). A plain automation runs in the generated application from its
automations screen and is not a model construct.

#### Loops

```yaml
loops:
  - id: L1
    condition: { id: lc1, field: retry_count, operator: lt, value: "5" }
    maxPasses: "10"
steps:
  - { id: s1, type: REST, resultName: "", props: { method: POST, url: https://lims.example.com/sync }, loopId: L1 }
  - { id: s2, type: UpdateEntity, resultName: "", props: { field: retry_count, value: "{{L1.iteration}}" }, loopId: L1 }
```

The steps carrying a loop's id run in order and repeat for as long as its
condition holds; the loop ends the first time it fails. **The condition is
re-read before every pass**, against the record as it stands then — a step inside
the loop changes the record, and that change is what ends it. It uses the same
eleven operators as conditions.

**`maxPasses` is required.** A while-loop is genuinely unbounded, and an
automation runs inside the write that triggered it: a condition that never fails
holds a database transaction open until something times out. There is no default
and no engine-wide constant — a retry that should give up after 5 and a
reconciliation that legitimately runs 800 cannot share one number. After
`maxPasses` passes the loop is abandoned and the run marked `FAILED`, naming the
loop and the limit. A loop with none is refused by the builder and warned about
by the compiler; an executor meeting one anyway runs a single pass.

**The condition must be able to change.** A loop whose condition reads a field no
member step writes is refused when the model compiles — it would read the same on
every pass. The check matches `UpdateEntity` writes by field name and treats every
other step type as able to change anything, so it reports only what it is sure
of.

Loops do not nest: a step carries at most one `loopId`. Inside a loop a step also
sees `{{<loopId>.iteration}}`, the 1-based pass number; a value published inside
the loop holds what the last pass left.

### 5.5 Combining them

One entity can carry all of it: columns and relationships (structure), `rules`
(declarative logic), `hooks` (imperative side effects), a state machine (its
lifecycle), `rbac` (who may do what) and sagas (the processes it starts). Keeping
them in one document makes the entity's whole behaviour reviewable in one place,
and the model viewer draws each of them from that document. See
`../yaml/examples/crm.eml.yaml` (`language/yaml/examples/crm.eml.yaml`) for a model that
uses every construct.

---

## 6. Access control — `rbac`

```yaml
rbac:
  - { entity: Account, action: read, roles: [sales_rep, sales_manager, support_agent] }
  - { entity: Opportunity, action: read, roles: [sales_rep, sales_manager] }
  - { entity: Opportunity, action: delete, roles: [sales_manager] }
  - { entity: Quote, action: approve, roles: [sales_manager] }
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **`entity`** | The entity the rule is about (`EML213` when undeclared). |
| **`action`** | A CRUD operation, `*` for all four, or a transition's `trigger` (`EML214` when it is neither). |
| **`roles`** | The roles that may perform it. |

Compiled by `packages/generator/src/rbac/` into `seed/access.sql` and enforced
by the generated backend's `services/authz.rs` on every `/api/bus/*` request.
An access rule that does not compile is an **error**, never a warning: it is a
restriction its author believes is in place and is not.

### It restricts; it does not grant

A target no rule mentions is **open** to any authenticated caller. One or more
rules close it to the union of the roles they name. A model that says nothing
about permissions belongs to an author who has not got to them yet, not to one
who wants everything forbidden — the opposite reading would lock every user out
of every existing model on its next regeneration.

A **master role** (`sys_role.is_master_role`) bypasses every access rule — but
not a state machine's topology, which binds everyone (§5.2).
Role names are matched **case-insensitively**: seeded roles are title-cased
(`Sales Manager`) and rules are written the model's way (`sales_manager`), and
an exact match would make such a rule unsatisfiable, locking out precisely the
people it was written to admit.

### CRUD operations and transitions

**CRUD**: `create`, `read`, `update`, `delete`, or `*` for all four. Aliases are
accepted: `insert`/`add`, `view`/`select`/`list`, `edit`/`write`/`modify`,
`remove`/`destroy`.

**Transitions**: any other action is resolved against the `trigger`s of the
entity's state machine. A generated application has no named-transition endpoint
— moving a record along an edge is an ordinary status update — so the rule is
stored as the `(from_state, to_state)` pairs its trigger covers, and the guard
recognises the move by the states a write crosses. Both ends are kept because one
trigger can sit on several edges and two triggers can reach the same state:
restricting `approve` must not incidentally restrict a different trigger that
lands on `approved`.

```yaml
stateMachines:
  - name: QuoteLifecycle
    entity: Quote
    states: [draft, pending, approved]
    transitions:
      - { from: draft, to: pending, trigger: submit }
      - { from: pending, to: approved, trigger: approve }

rbac:
  - { entity: Quote, action: approve, roles: [sales_manager] }
```

### `read` decides whose an entity is

Every other operation only refuses a write. `read` is the one that changes what a
role *sees*: an entity a role may not read is absent from that role's navigation
— no menu entry, no dashboard card, no lookup — because a menu full of entries
that answer 403 is a worse application than a shorter one. One `read` rule per
entity is how a model says who the entity belongs to, and a model is expected to
name **every** entity in at least one. Declaring none leaves every entity visible
to every signed-in caller: the fallback, not the target.

Three things follow, and each has caught a model out:

- **A role that may act on an entity must also be able to read it.** A rule
  letting `sales_manager` `approve` a quote is useless if the quote's `read` rule
  does not name `sales_manager`.
- **Overlap is normal.** An `Account` belongs to sales, marketing and support in
  most businesses; name all three. Two rules on one target merge.
- **Do not reach for `*` to express ownership.** It restricts creating, updating
  and deleting to the same list, and it *merges with* rather than overrides the
  narrower rules on the same entity — widening them.

### One account per role

Every role a rule names is created, and one account is seeded holding it,
beside the administrator — who bypasses everything — and a role-less user. An
application whose only account is the administrator is one whose access control
cannot be looked at. The role accounts share `ROLE_ACCOUNT_PASSWORD` (default
`admin`), and a re-run of the seed does not reset them. Both generators derive
the list the same way (`packages/generator/src/rbac/roles.ts`,
`crates/appwithai-gen/src/rbac.rs`).

### What it compiles to

| | |
|---|---|
| CRUD rules | `sys_operation_access` (table, operation, role) |
| Transition rules | `sys_transition_access` (table, trigger, status column, from, to, role) |
| Roles | every role named, in `sys_role`, each granted the business windows in `sys_access` |
| `read` rules | additionally narrow the dashboard and the navigation to the roles named |
| Enforcement | `services/authz.rs`: `sys_access`, then the operation rules, then the transition rules |

Rows seeded from the model are **model-managed**: regeneration replaces what the
model owns without discarding what an administrator added in the running
application. Every gate denies when it cannot read its rules — a restriction that
disappears under load is not a restriction.

---

## 7. Reports and triggers

### Reports

```yaml
reports:
  - name: unassigned-jobs
    title: Jobs with no engineer
    entity: Job
    help: The dispatcher's first question every morning.
    sql: |
      SELECT reference, scheduled_for
        FROM bus_job
       WHERE engineer_id IS NULL
       ORDER BY scheduled_for
  - name: orders_by_status
    title: Orders by status
    entity: Order
    chart: bar
    x: status
    y: count
    sql: SELECT status, count(*) AS count FROM bus_order GROUP BY status
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **`name`** | The report's key, unique (`EML292`: a duplicate would silently replace the earlier one). |
| `title`, `help` | What the reports list shows. |
| `entity` | The entity it is mainly about; groups it in the list (`EML295` when undeclared). |
| `chart` | `bar`, `line`, `pie` or `area`; requires `x` and `y`, the result columns it plots. |
| **`sql`** | One `SELECT` or `WITH` statement, as a block scalar when it spans lines. |

A report is a question the application's users actually ask, written down as the
SQL that answers it. Structure alone yields a register per entity and a breakdown
per enum; nothing in an entity list says that a dispatcher's first question is
which jobs have no engineer. A report is where that knowledge lives, so it
travels with the model.

Compiled to `sys_report` (`packages/generator/src/reports/`, and
`crates/appwithai-gen/src/reports.rs`) and served at `/api/reports`, capped at
5,000 rows by an outer `LIMIT` over the query, so the model's own ordering still
decides which rows.

**A report may only read**, and that is refused three times: by the schema and
checker at authoring time (`EML293`), by the compiler before the query can reach
a seed file, and by the generated controller before it runs — `sys_report` is an
ordinary table, so the reader does not trust what it is handed. The check tracks
quoting rather than scanning for a keyword: `SELECT 1; DROP TABLE bus_user` opens
with a `SELECT`. A single trailing semicolon is allowed; a second statement is
not. Anything that writes belongs in a rule or a hook.

The query runs against the generated application's database, so it names `bus_`
tables, and joins keys plainly — primary and foreign keys are both UUIDs, so
`ON c.account_id = a.id` needs no cast.

### Triggers

```yaml
triggers:
  - { entity: Quote, source: "cron:0 0 * * *", handler: expireQuotes }
  - { entity: Order, source: "webhook:payment", handler: markPaid }
  - { entity: Shipment, source: "message:carrier-updates", handler: recordScan }
```

An external event or schedule that calls `handler` on `entity`. `source` is
`cron:<5 or 6 fields>` (`EML231` otherwise), `webhook:<name>` or
`message:<topic>`; quote it, since a cron expression contains spaces and a
`:`. Triggers are **validated** — the schema and checker enforce their shape and
their entity (`EML232`) — and the `eml` CLI's generators compile them; the
TanStack/Loco application generators do not yet.

---

## 8. Validation — the published validator

One ES module, at a fixed URL, and two runners beside it. The module is bundled
from the same reader, schema, checker and fixer the command line runs — not a
lighter web edition — so a document that passes here is a document the generator
will accept.

| File | URL | What it gives you |
|---|---|---|
| `model-yaml.js` | `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/model-yaml.js` | `validate(text)` — YAML syntax, the JSON Schema and the full checker, every finding at its YAML line and column — and `fix(text)`, the eight auto-repairs with a re-check |
| `check-model.mjs` | `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/check-model.mjs` | §1.3's three passes as one command (§8.4) |
| `audit-model.mjs` | `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/audit-model.mjs` | the twenty-two-point checklist audit (§8.5) |

### 8.1 The API

```js
import { validate, fix, LANGUAGE_VERSION }
  from "https://www.appwithai.org/guide/model-yaml.js";
```

`validate(text)` returns:

```
{
  ok: boolean,                 // no errors; warnings may remain
  document,                    // the model as read — present when the YAML parsed
  diagnostics: [
    { severity, code, message, path, line, column, hint }
  ]
}
```

`path` is where in the document the finding is — `["entities", 0,
"attributes", 1]` — and `line` and `column` are where that is in your text.
`hint` says what to change; most diagnostics carry one.

`fix(text)` repairs what it can **in the YAML text itself, keeping its comments
and its layout**, re-checks the result, and returns:

```
{
  text,          // the document as it should now be used
  applied: [ { code, path, description } ],   // what was repaired, in order
  diagnostics,   // what is still there — none of it auto-repairable
  ok
}
```

`LANGUAGE_VERSION` is the language definition's version, `2.0.0`.

**Line numbers belong to the text that was checked.** `fix` can add a line — a
missing `name`, a missing key — so every `line` in its `diagnostics` indexes
`result.text`, not the string you passed in. Use the returned text, or validate
again after writing it, before you act on a line number.

### 8.2 Severities and code bands

**error** — the generator would produce something wrong, or nothing. Do not deliver.
**warning** — legal, but almost certainly not what was meant. Clear it or explain it.
**info** — an observation worth reading once. It never fails a run, and a report
carrying nothing worse than infos is a report on a model that passed.

The runners print the diagnostics first and **the verdict last**, so the final
line is always the outcome:

```
OK — 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes (EML 2.0.0)
```

or `FAILED — …` with the counts beside it. Read that line, not the last
diagnostic above it: an `info` has the same shape as an error, and the run it
belongs to may well have passed.

| Band | Where the fault is |
|---|---|
| `YAML` | Not YAML at all, or a key written twice |
| `SCHEMA` | Valid YAML that is not a model document — a missing required key, a value of the wrong shape, a key the language does not have |
| `EML001`–`EML099` | The document: its name, its emptiness |
| `EML100`–`EML119` | Entities and attributes |
| `EML120`–`EML129` | Relationships |
| `EML130`–`EML199` | Enums and their bindings, entity help, icons and parents, indexes, categories |
| `EML200`–`EML299` | Hooks, access rules, triggers, reports and saga steps |
| `EML300`–`EML399` | Business rules: decision graphs and actions |
| `EML400`–`EML449` | Workflows: state machines, sagas and hook flows |
| `EML500`–`EML599` | Cross-construct consistency — two parts of the model disagreeing |

**`YAML` and `SCHEMA` on a first attempt are almost always the wrong bytes**, not
a model with a typo in it: a specification, a summary, a Markdown answer with
the model in a fenced block, a path instead of a file's contents, or a model that
was described and never written. `SCHEMA: document must be object` is a
paragraph; `YAML` errors on the lines of a bullet list are Markdown. Check what
you passed in, then §1.2. Editing the prose never fixes it.

### 8.3 The eight auto-repairs

These, and only these, `fix` will repair without being told what was meant.
Everything else needs a decision, which is why it is handed back untouched.

| Code | Fault | Repair |
|---|---|---|
| `EML001` | The model has no `name` | Sets one, derived from the first entity |
| `EML103` | A column the generator adds anyway | Removes the declaration |
| `EML112` | The same column declared twice | Removes the later one, keeping the stronger constraints |
| `EML114` | An `fk` column not ending `_id` | Appends the suffix — in the attribute, its indexes and hook fields |
| `EML117` | An entity with no primary key that declares `id` or a `*_id` column — so the generator cannot add its own `id` | Marks its `id` column as the key, or adds `id` as a uuid primary key |
| `EML287` | A rule condition naming a camelCase identifier | Rewrites it as the snake_case column |
| `EML421` | A state machine with no `initial` | Sets it to the machine's first state |
| `EML422` | A state machine with no `final` | Sets it to the states that have no way out |

`EML287` is repaired for a reason worth knowing. A rule reads the record being
written, whose keys are the model's column names, and every column is
snake_case — so `when: encounterId == null` compares `undefined` to `null`,
which is true, and the rule refuses **every** write to that entity. The mirror
case, `when: isCritical == true`, compares `undefined` to `true` and the rule
never fires at all: seeded, listed in the admin screen, drawn by the viewer, and
inert. Neither reports anything at run time, and the repair — the snake_case
spelling of the same name — needs no decision.

`EML103` and `EML112` are repaired rather than reported-and-left because both
produced the same fatal outcome: a `CREATE TABLE` naming one column twice, which
PostgreSQL refuses, so the generated application never opened. **A duplicate
keeps the strongest of the two declarations, never the last one**: a column
declared required and then `optional: true` stays required, because relaxing a
mandatory column is invisible in a review and surfaces much later as missing
data. `unique` and `fk` carry over the same way.

Prefer fixing these yourself. The repair is mechanical and cannot know that the
primary key should have been a natural one, or that the model's name is the
customer's brand rather than its first entity.

`EML114` can leave a new diagnostic behind: renaming a column changes what its
name resolves to (§3.5), so an `EML502` can appear where the warning was.
Re-read the report after a repair; do not assume the count only falls.

### 8.4 Running the validator where you are

The validator is one ES module on a public URL. Loading it is one line on some
runtimes and several on others, and that difference is where the validation step
usually gets skipped. Find your row and run it.

| What you have | What to do |
|---|---|
| A shell with Node 18+, Bun or Deno | `curl -sO https://www.appwithai.org/guide/check-model.mjs` then `node check-model.mjs <business-name>.eml.yaml` |
| Bun or Deno, writing the code yourself | `import { validate, fix } from "https://www.appwithai.org/guide/model-yaml.js"` — a URL import works as it stands |
| Node, writing the code yourself | Node has no network imports: fetch the module, write it into a directory, `import()` it from there (below) |
| A browser, a canvas, an HTML preview | `<script type="module">` with the same URL import — or paste the document into `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/11-check-a-model.html`, which runs this same module in the tab. Either is a real run and its counts are reportable |
| A browse or fetch tool **beside** a shell with no network | The split most assistants have, and a bridge rather than a blocker. Read `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/model-yaml.js` with the layer that can reach it, write it into the shell's working directory — a heredoc will do, and a file too large for one write goes in pieces — then run the first row with `--base .`. The shell needs no network, only a file write |
| A fetch layer that reads **pages** but refuses `application/javascript` | Commoner than it sounds, and it reports the module as inaccessible while the same host serves it pages without complaint — which reads as the site being broken. The module and both runners are published inside pages for exactly this: `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/source/` links one page per file, each carrying that file base64-encoded with its SHA-256. Read the page, strip whitespace, `base64 -d`, check the hash, then the row above. Base64 is used rather than escaped source because it survives a reflow or a Markdown conversion — and because a corrupted copy then fails the hash instead of quietly becoming a validator that is not this one |
| A shell that runs Node but **reaches no host at all**, and a text-only way in | **One file.** `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/check-model-standalone.mjs` carries `model-yaml.js` and **both** runners compressed inside it. Get that one file there by any means — paste it, print it from a layer that can read it, copy it off another machine — then `node check-model-standalone.mjs <business-name>.eml.yaml`, and add `--audit` for §8.5's checklist score. It inflates them into a temp directory and runs the published runners against them: same three passes, same diagnostics, same `0`/`1`/`2`. **A real run, counts reportable.** The published files are smaller apart than this is together, so prefer them whenever anything can fetch |
| A shell, but **no egress** — a sandbox, a proxy, an air-gapped runner | The validator is one dependency-free file, and both `check-model.mjs` and `audit-model.mjs` prefer a local copy of it to the network. Put `model-yaml.js` in the directory you are working in, or beside the script, or name its directory with `--base <dir>` — a relative directory such as `--base ./` is fine — and run them exactly as above. **This is a real run**: same engine, same report, same exit codes, counts reportable |
| No JavaScript runtime at all | Walk §10 by hand, and say in your delivery that the model was checked against the checklist and not against the validator |

**A blocked network is not a failed validation, and it is not a stopping
point.** An agent sandbox usually reports it as a DNS failure or as a gateway
error — 403, 407, 502 — and both read like the site being down when the site is
answering everyone else. Work the rows above in order and stop at the first that
runs; reach the last row by exhausting the others, not by inferring it. `curl`
returning nothing is one attempt with one host, not the end of the ladder.

**Classify the failure by its exit code before you describe it.** These mean
different things, and only one of them is about the site at all:

| What you see | What it is | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| `curl: (6)` · `EAI_AGAIN` · `ENOTFOUND` | The host did not resolve | **There is no working DNS here.** Nothing was sent. Resolve any other host to confirm — if that fails too, the resolver is the finding, and it is not about this hostname |
| `curl: (7)` · `ECONNREFUSED` | Resolved, nothing accepted the connection | Egress is blocked at the network layer. Nothing was sent |
| `curl: (56)` with `403` or `407` | A proxy refused the CONNECT | Your gateway answered, in the site's place. Nothing was sent |
| `403` · `407` · `502` with a body | An HTTP answer that is not the site's | Same: an egress proxy or corporate gateway replying for it |
| `404` from this host | The site answered, and that path is wrong | The only one of these that is a fact about the site. Re-read the URL |

The first four never reached the site, so none of them is evidence it is down,
and none is a verdict on the model. Say which one you got, verbatim, and go on
to the offline rows — they are real runs.

**"My web layer can read it, my shell cannot" is a bridge, not a verdict.** It
is the commonest split there is: a browsing or fetch tool that reaches the
module, beside a sandboxed shell that cannot resolve the host. Both halves of the
job are present — one side reads, the other writes a file and runs Node — so read
the module with the side that reaches and write it where the side that runs will
find it. Naming the split and stopping is describing the transport, not the
validator.

**And whatever happens, do not stall.** If you cannot obtain a validator result,
finish the work and say so in one sentence — *"delivered unvalidated: the
published validator was unreachable from this environment (403 from the proxy),
so these counts are absent rather than estimated"*. What you must never do is
invent counts, and what you must not do instead is hold the work open waiting for
a host that this environment is never going to reach. An unvalidated model
delivered with that sentence attached is useful; a protocol stopped at a gate is
not.

**Nothing here needs a checkout, and nothing here needs GitHub.** There is no
repository to clone, no credentials to hold and no `bun` to install: the module
and the runners are served from `https://www.appwithai.org`. `check-model.mjs`
resolves the module from `--base`, then from its own directory, then from the
working directory, then from `./guide/`, then from the published site — GitHub
is in none of those paths. "I could not obtain the repository, therefore I could
not validate" is a wrong inference, not an honest limitation, and it has been
observed in the wild.

**Write the URL in full, every time: `https://www.appwithai.org/…`.** Scheme
included, `www.` included, never a bare host. Three things go wrong otherwise and
all three have been observed:

- **A bare host is not a URL.** `appwithai.org/guide/model-yaml.js` is a string a
  runtime either refuses or has to guess a scheme for, and a sandboxed agent's
  HTTP client usually refuses.
- **A Markdown link around a bare host is worse**, because it looks right.
  `[appwithai.org](https://www.appwithai.org)` reads to a person as a working
  link and to anything parsing your output as the bare host. Write the plain
  absolute URL: this is a specification, not a web page, and nothing here is
  rendered.
- **The apex is not the canonical form.** `https://appwithai.org/…` serves the
  same files and is the domain the repository's `CNAME` pins, but
  `https://www.appwithai.org/…` is the canonical form to write. Both carry a
  certificate; write the canonical one so every reference agrees.

**The same rule governs how you report a failure.** Name the exact request and
the exact error. *"Validator retrieval failed for appwithai.org"* says neither
what was requested nor what happened; *"GET
https://www.appwithai.org/guide/model-yaml.js failed: EAI_AGAIN (DNS)"* says
both, and is the difference between a reader who can reproduce your problem and
one who cannot. Report the URL you actually requested — not a shortened,
prettified or linked version of it.

**What a diagnostic gives you back.** Every diagnostic carries its code, the
YAML line and column, the message and, usually, a hint; `validate` also returns
the document path. The runner prints each one like this:

```
warn  EML146:8:9  Column "Order.status" names no enum.
      → Declare  { name: OrderStatus, values: [...] }  under  enums:  and set  enum: OrderStatus  on the column. Without it the dictionary records free text, and the form accepts values the state machine cannot act on.
```

Match your edit against what the message names — the entity and the column —
rather than against the line number alone. If line 8 in your copy is not
`Order.status`, you are editing a different document from the one that was
checked — which is the commonest way a fix gets reported as applied when it
never was.

**The same mistake generalises, and it has now been made three ways.** Not
reaching GitHub, not reaching `llmdetailed.txt` itself, and Node refusing a URL
import are each one address or one call failing. None of them is a statement
about `guide/model-yaml.js`, which is a different file on a different host — and
`check-model.mjs` needs no specification document at all: it reads the model and
nothing else. Whatever you could not fetch, walk the ladder before reporting the
validator as unavailable. Re-reading this text is not a precondition for running
the engine it describes.

**Perform the validation; do not offer it.** "If you want the actual counts, I
can run the published validator" hands the user a choice they were never given:
the run is required, so the counts are part of the deliverable rather than an
upgrade to it. A model that proposes the mandatory step instead of taking it has
skipped it — and the offer reads as diligence, which is what makes it hard to
catch.

```sh
curl -sO https://www.appwithai.org/guide/check-model.mjs
node check-model.mjs my-business.eml.yaml
```

**`check-model.mjs`** is the one-command form of §1.3, published beside the
module it runs. It finds `model-yaml.js` as described above, runs `fix` and then
two `validate` passes over the repaired bytes, prints every finding, and exits
`0` when the model is clean, `1` when the generator would refuse it, `2` when it
could not run at all. `--write` saves the repaired document back over the input;
`--base <dir-or-url>` points it at another copy; `--quiet` prints the verdict
line alone. It is a runner, not a second validator: every finding it prints comes
from the published module.

In Node, written by hand:

```js
import { writeFileSync, mkdtempSync, readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { pathToFileURL } from "node:url";

const dir = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), "eml-"));
const response = await fetch("https://www.appwithai.org/guide/model-yaml.js");
writeFileSync(join(dir, "model-yaml.js"), await response.text());
const { validate, fix } = await import(pathToFileURL(join(dir, "model-yaml.js")).href);

const repaired = fix(readFileSync("my-business.eml.yaml", "utf8"));
const result = validate(repaired.text);
for (const d of result.diagnostics) console.log(d.severity, d.code, `${d.line}:${d.column}`, d.message);
console.log(result.ok ? "OK" : "FAILED");
```

### 8.5 Is the model *finished*? — the checklist audit

A clean report and a finished model are different things, and the gap between
them is where delivered models actually fail.

Nothing in the validator requires a model to *have* anything. A single entity
with a primary key and a name is a valid model: no state machine, no saga, no
hook, no rule `actions`, no `rbac` entry, not one word of help text — zero
errors, and the generator will build it. What comes out is a grid of text boxes
that every user can see all of, with no lifecycle, no rules and no security, and
the report said it was fine. The warnings that do fire (`EML146`, `EML152`,
`EML153`) are warnings: the verdict line still reads `OK`, which is true and is
not the same as *"this model is done"*.

So there is a second published runner, beside the first and resolved the same
way:

```sh
curl -sO https://www.appwithai.org/guide/audit-model.mjs
node audit-model.mjs my-business.eml.yaml
```

It scores the mechanical half of §1.2's file contract and §10's checklist —
twenty-two checks — and its last line is the score:

```
22 passed, 0 failed
```

Exit `0` when every check passed, `1` when one or more failed, `2` when it could
not run. `--quiet` prints the score line alone; `--base <dir-or-url>` is the same
flag `check-model.mjs` has, and the offline rows of §8.4 apply unchanged.

What it holds a model to, and what a clean validator run would not have told
you:

| It checks | Because a clean report does not mean |
|---|---|
| The file's name, its first line, no Markdown fences or second documents in it | The bytes are one `.eml.yaml` document, not prose about one (§1.2) |
| Every entity has a primary key; every `fk` column ends `_id`; **every reference column carries `fk: true`** | The reference is a `Table Direct` lookup rather than a silently downgraded text box (§3.7) |
| Every `status`/`state`/`stage` column is bound to an enum | The control is a List rather than free text the state machine cannot act on (§3.7) |
| At least one state machine, each with an `initial` and a `final` state | The records have a lifecycle at all (§5.2) |
| Rule `actions`, `sagas`, `hooks` and `rbac` are all present | The model decides, runs and restricts something — rather than being a list of tables |
| Help on every entity and every column, **none of it restating its own name** | The application and its generated manual say something. `Status for Client.` is complete coverage and worthless (`EML151`, `EML152`, `EML153`) |
| Every declared line item is out of every category, and every candidate is reported | The dashboard does not carry a card listing every invoice line ever written (§3.5.1, `EML149`, `EML150`) |
| `fix` then two `validate` passes over the repaired bytes, all clean, and no repair outstanding | The bytes you are delivering are the bytes that passed (§1.3) |

Three of those — `fk: true`, the enum binding, and help that says something —
are the ones worth re-reading, because each is a warning the generator proceeds
past after quietly getting the application wrong.

**It is a scorer, not a second validator.** Every diagnostic it reads comes from
`model-yaml.js`; it adds no codes of its own. And it cannot tell you the model
says what the business meant — only that nothing in it is mechanically
unfinished. `EML149` candidates are *printed* rather than counted against the
score, because whether something is a line item is a question about the business
and a candidate you have considered and rejected is a legitimate answer.

**Run it before you deliver, and report its score beside the validator's
counts.** A delivery that says *"0 errors, 0 warnings"* and nothing else is not
wrong, and it is not the whole truth about the file either.

---

## 9. A complete worked example

A CRM, cut down to the three entities a lead-to-account conversion needs. The
full model — seventeen entities, five state machines, five sagas, thirty-two
access rules — is published at `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/models/crm.eml.yaml`,
and chapter 09 of the guide generates it and runs it in a browser tab:
`https://www.appwithai.org/guide/run-in-browser.html`.

### 9.1 The model

```yaml
eml: "1.0"
name: Enterprise CRM
version: 1.0.0

enums:
  - name: UserRole
    values: [administrator, sales_rep, marketing_manager]
  - name: LeadStatus
    values: [new, working, qualified, converted, disqualified]
  - name: LeadSource
    values: [web, referral, event, partner]
  - name: LeadRating
    values: [hot, warm, cold]

categories:
  - name: Marketing
    description: Campaigns and the leads they generate
    icon: Megaphone
    entities: [Campaign, Lead]
  - name: Administration
    description: The people who use the application
    icon: Settings
    entities: [User]

entities:
  - name: User
    help: Someone who signs in and does the work — a rep, a manager, a marketer. Every business record names one as its owner.
    attributes:
      - { name: id, type: string, pk: true }
      - name: email
        type: email
        unique: true
        help: The address this user signs in with. It must be unique across the application.
      - name: full_name
        type: string
        help: The name shown on screen and in email.
      - name: role
        type: string
        enum: UserRole
        help: What this user is allowed to do. The role decides which records they can see at all.
  - name: Campaign
    help: A marketing programme with a budget and a window, run to generate leads.
    attributes:
      - { name: id, type: string, pk: true }
      - name: name
        type: string
        help: What this programme is called in reporting.
      - name: start_date
        type: date
        help: The day the campaign goes live.
      - name: budgeted_cost
        type: decimal
        optional: true
        help: What marketing agreed to spend on this programme.
  - name: Lead
    help: An unqualified enquiry that has not been connected to an account yet. A lead is either converted or disqualified.
    audited: true
    attributes:
      - { name: id, type: string, pk: true }
      - name: company_name
        type: string
        help: The company they said they were from. It becomes the account name on conversion.
      - name: employee_count
        type: int
        optional: true
        help: Head count as the lead reported it; the largest single input to the score.
      - name: lead_source
        type: string
        enum: LeadSource
        help: Where the enquiry came from. Referrals score highest.
      - name: score
        type: int
        optional: true
        help: The qualification score, 0 to 100, computed when the lead is captured.
      - name: rating
        type: string
        enum: LeadRating
        optional: true
        help: Hot, warm or cold, read off the score so a rep can sort the queue at a glance.
      - name: status
        type: string
        enum: LeadStatus
        help: Where this lead has got to, from new through to converted or disqualified.
      - name: campaign_id
        type: string
        fk: true
        optional: true
        help: The campaign that produced this lead, when one did.
      - name: owner_id
        type: string
        fk: true
        help: The user working this lead.
    indexes:
      - columns: [owner_id, status]

relationships:
  - { from: Campaign, fromCardinality: exactly-one, to: Lead, toCardinality: zero-or-more, label: generates }
  - { from: User, fromCardinality: exactly-one, to: Lead, toCardinality: zero-or-more, label: owns }

stateMachines:
  - name: LeadLifecycle
    entity: Lead
    title: Lead Lifecycle
    states: [new, working, qualified, converted, disqualified]
    initial: new
    final: [converted, disqualified]
    transitions:
      - { from: new, to: working, trigger: start_work }
      - { from: working, to: qualified, trigger: qualify }
      - { from: working, to: disqualified, trigger: disqualify }
      - { from: qualified, to: converted, trigger: convert }

rules:
  - name: leadScoring
    title: Lead Scoring
    entity: Lead
    event: beforeCreate
    priority: 10
    nodes:
      - { id: A, label: "Start: Lead Captured", type: start }
      - { id: B, label: employee_count >= 1000?, type: decision }
      - { id: C, label: Add 35 firmographic points, type: expression }
      - { id: D, label: Add 5 firmographic points, type: expression }
      - { id: E, label: Compute lead score, type: function }
      - { id: Z, label: "End: Lead Scored", type: end }
    edges:
      - { from: A, to: B }
      - { from: B, to: C, label: "Yes" }
      - { from: B, to: D, label: "No" }
      - { from: C, to: E }
      - { from: D, to: E }
      - { from: E, to: Z }
  - name: leadQualification
    title: Lead Qualification
    entity: Lead
    event: beforeUpdate
    priority: 15
    nodes:
      - { id: A, label: "Start: Lead Updated", type: start }
      - { id: B, label: status == qualified?, type: decision }
      - { id: Z, label: "End: Lead Routed", type: end }
    edges:
      - { from: A, to: B }
      - { from: B, to: Z, label: "Yes" }
      - { from: B, to: Z, label: "No" }
    actions:
      - name: convertQualifiedLead
        type: trigger-workflow
        when: status == "qualified"
        props:
          workflow: LeadConversion
          message: Lead qualified — converting it

sagas:
  - name: LeadConversion
    title: Lead Conversion
    entity: Lead
    trigger: rule
    steps:
      - id: B
        type: UpdateEntity
        label: Mark the lead converted
        properties:
          field: status
          value: converted

rbac:
  - entity: Campaign
    action: read
    roles: [marketing_manager]
  - entity: Lead
    action: read
    roles: [sales_rep, marketing_manager]
  - entity: Lead
    action: convert
    roles: [sales_rep]
```

That is a complete model, not an excerpt: it validates with no diagnostics and
generates a running application. The full CRM grows it to seventeen entities, but
the shape does not change. One file, one document. Every construct sits under its
own key, so an entity's whole behaviour — its columns, its rules, its lifecycle,
who may touch it — is found by its name rather than by position.

### 9.2 Watch it run — the chain end to end

One user action, eight links, every one of them declared in the model:

| # | What runs | Declared as |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | a user sets `status = qualified` | a value of the `LeadStatus` enum |
| 2 | `leadQualification` evaluates | `rules: [{ name: leadQualification, entity: Lead, event: beforeUpdate }]` |
| 3 | its action fires | `actions: [{ type: trigger-workflow, when: status == "qualified", props: { workflow: LeadConversion } }]` |
| 4 | `LeadConversion` starts | `sagas: [{ name: LeadConversion, trigger: rule }]` |
| 5 | a decision table sizes the account | step `B`, `type: Decision` |
| 6 | Account, Contact, Opportunity created | steps `C`–`E`, `type: CreateEntity` |
| 7 | the lead is marked converted | step `F`, `type: UpdateEntity` |
| 8 | the account's tier is stamped | step `G`, `type: UpdateEntity` with `targetSource` |

---

## 10. Before you deliver — the checklist

**Most of this list is machine-checkable, so do not walk it by hand.** Items 1-4
and 6-16 are what `audit-model.mjs` scores — twenty-two checks, one command, the
same engine the validator runs (§8.5):

```sh
curl -sO https://www.appwithai.org/guide/audit-model.mjs
node audit-model.mjs my-business.eml.yaml
```

`22 passed, 0 failed` and exit `0` is the state to deliver in. Read the list
anyway for the three items no script can answer — 5, 7 and 17 are about whether
the model matches the business — and for the reasoning behind the ones it can.

**The file itself**

1. There *is* a file, and it is one YAML document — not a document describing
   one (§1.0).
2. It opens with `eml: "1.0"`, and declares `name` and `entities`.
3. It contains no Markdown, no fences, no prose outside `#` comments, and no
   second YAML document.
4. It is one file, named `<business-name>.eml.yaml`.

**The model**

5. Every entity from the enhanced specification (§1.1) is in the document.
6. Every entity has a primary key you chose, declares each column once
   (`EML112`), and declares none of the columns the generator adds (§3.1,
   `EML103`).
7. Every entity that something references has a `name`, `title` or `code`
   column — that is what a lookup and a grid show in place of the uuid (§3.7).
8. Every foreign key ends `_id`, **carries `fk: true`**, and has a matching
   entry in `relationships` — the flag is what makes it a `Table Direct` lookup
   in the Application Dictionary rather than a text box (§3.7).
9. Every status column, and every other column with a closed vocabulary, is
   bound with `enum:` to an entry in `enums` — without the binding the
   dictionary records free text (§3.7).
10. **Every entity carries `help` and every column carries `help`** — no
   exceptions, including the self-evident ones, and the primary key the one
   thing that needs none. That text is the whole of the application's help *and*
   the whole of its generated manual, and no later pass adds it (§3.1, §3.7).
   **It has to be domain knowledge, not the name in a sentence**: `Status for
   Client.` passes a coverage check and tells a reader nothing. Clear every
   `EML151` (help that restates its subject), `EML152` (an entity with none) and
   `EML153` (columns with none).
11. **Every line item is declared as one.** Go through the entities and ask of
   each: is this a thing in its own right, or part of another thing? Every
   invoice line, order line, prescription item and delivery line gets
   `parent: <Parent>`, and is left out of `categories` (§3.5.1). Missing it puts
   a card on the dashboard listing every line ever written, which is a screen
   nobody opens — and leaves the parent record with no sign of its own lines.
   The validator names every candidate it can see as `EML149`; walk each one and
   either declare the parent or decide against it, and clear any `EML150` by
   taking the child out of its category.
12. Every entity with a status has an entry in `stateMachines`, with an
   `initial` and a `final` state.
13. Every rule that must *do* something has `actions` — not just a decision.
14. Every cross-entity effect is a hook, a rule action, or a saga step.
15. Every restricted operation and transition has an `rbac` entry.
16. Every entity is named by at least one `rbac` entry with `action: read`, so it
   belongs to a functional role — and every role that may act on an entity can
   also read it (§6). A model where one role sees all forty tables is the same
   application once, not four times.
17. **If the model carries `reports`, more than one role has them.** A reporting
   layer that answers one person's questions is that person's saved query. Walk
   the roles against the `rbac` entries: a role that can read records and has no
   report can see its records and cannot ask anything about them. Reports are
   optional — a model without any is complete — but a model with exactly one
   role's worth is half-finished rather than economical.

**The handover**

18. Exactly one file is being handed over, and it ends `.eml.yaml` — no
    companion specification document, report or README (§1.0).
19. `validate(text)` returns `ok: true`, run three times over the file's exact
    bytes, the last two over unchanged bytes — `node check-model.mjs
    <file>.eml.yaml` is those three passes and exits `0` — and you reached that
    state by looping validate → fix → validate until the report was empty, for
    at least 10 cycles or until it came back clean, whichever was first (§1.3) —
    or you have said plainly that the validator could not be run and walked this
    list by hand instead (§1.3).
20. Warnings are cleared, or each remaining one is explained to the user.
21. **`node audit-model.mjs <file>.eml.yaml` exits `0`** — every mechanical item
    above, scored rather than remembered (§8.5). A clean validator run does not
    imply this one: a model with no `rbac`, no state machine and no help text is
    0 errors, and it is not finished. If a check fails and you are leaving it
    that way, say which and why.
22. The file the user receives is the file you validated, delivered as a
    download, with the enhanced specification, the validator counts **and the
    audit score** beside it in the reply — not inside the file (§1.4).
